'''vilifier''' (vil′i-fī-ėr), ''n.'' [< ''vilify'' + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] One who defames or traduces; a calumniator.

'''vilify''' (vil′i-fī), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''vilified'', ppr. ''vilifying''. [< LL. ''vilificare'', < L. ''vilis'', vile, + ''-ficare'', < ''facere'', make: see ''-fy''.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To make vile; debase; degrade.
{{smaller block|<poem>Their Maker’s image . . . then
Forsook them, when themselves they ''vilified''
To serve ungoverned appetite.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., xi. 516.}}
The wealth and pride of individuals at every moment makes the man of humble rank and fortune sensible of his inferiority, and degrades and ''vilifies'' his condition.
{{right|''Burke'', Rev. in France.}}}}
'''2.''' To attempt to degrade by slander; defame; traduce; calumniate.
{{smaller block|<poem>This Tomalin could not abide
To hear his sovereign ''vilified''.</poem>
{{right|''Drayton'', Nymphidia.}}}}
'''3†.''' To treat as worthless, vile, or of no account.
{{smaller block|You shall not finde our Saviour . . . so bent to contemn and ''vilifie'' a poor suitor.
{{right|''Hales'', Remains, Sermon on Luke xviii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller|='''Syn. 2.''' ''Asperse'', ''Defame'', ''Calumniate'', etc. (see ''asperse''), revile, abuse.}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To utter slander; be guilty of defamation. ''Rev. T. Adams'', Works, I. 153.

'''vilifying''' (vil′i-fī-ing), ''n.'' [Verbal n. of ''vilify'', ''v.''] The act of defaming or traducing; defamation; slander.
{{smaller block|In the midst of all the storms and reproaches and ''vilifyings'' that the world heaps upon me.
{{right|''Sir M. Hale'', Preparation against Afflictions.}}}}

'''vil†''', ''n.'' Same as ''vill.''

'''vilayet''' (vil-a-yet′), ''n.'' [Turk. ''vilāyet'', < Ar. ''wilāya'', province, government, sovereignty.] An administrative territory of the first class; a province of the Turkish empire. {{smaller|Each Turkish vilayet is ruled by a vali, or governor-general. The division into vilayets has replaced the old system of eyalets.}}

'''vild†''', ''a.'' [A corrupt form of ''vile''. In some cases the word appears to have been confused with ''wild''.] Same as ''vile''.
{{smaller block|Be thy life ne’re so ''vilde''. ''Times’ Whistle'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 44.
<poem>What ''vild'' prisons
Make we our bodies to our immortal souls!</poem>
{{right|''Middleton and Rowley'', Spanish Gypsy, iii. 1.}}
My act, though ''vild'', the world shall crown as just.
{{right|''Dekker and Webster'', Westward Ho, iv. 2.}}}}

'''vildly†''', ''adv.'' Same as ''vilely''. ''Spenser'', F. Q., I. iii. 43.

'''vile''' (vīl), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [Early mod. E. also ''vyle'' (also ''vild'', q. v.); < ME. ''vile'', ''vil'', < OF. (and F.) ''vil'', fem. ''vile'' = Sp. Pg. ''vil'' = It. ''vile'', < L. ''vilis'', of small price or value, poor, paltry, base, vile.] '''I.''' ''a.'' '''1.''' Of small value; held in little esteem; low; base; mean; worthless; despicable.
{{smaller block|<poem>And the tre was ''vil'' and old.</poem>
{{right|''Holy Rood'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 34.}}
Running, leaping, and quoiting be too ''vile'' for scholars, and so not fit by Aristotle’s judgment.
{{right|''Ascham'', Toxophilus (ed. 1864), p. 34.}}
A poor man in ''vile'' raiment. {{right|Jas. ii. 2.}}
<poem>I never knew man hold ''vile'' stuff so dear.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', L. L. L., iv. 3. 276.}}}}

'''2.''' Morally base or impure; depraved; bad; wicked; abject; villainous; shameful: frequently used as an epithet of opprobrium, contempt, disgust, or odium generally.
{{smaller block|Wisdom and goodness to the ''vile'' seem ''vile''.
{{right|''Shak.'', Lear, iv. 2. 38.}}}}
{{smaller block|What can his censure hurt me whom the world
Hath censured ''vile'' before me!
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Cynthia’s Revels, iii. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|It were too ''vile'' to say, and scarce to be beleeued, what we endured.
{{right|Quoted in ''Capt. John Smith’s'' Works, II. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|Rendering those who receive the allowance ''vile'', and of no estimation in the eyes of mankind.
{{right|''Burke'', Rev. in France.}}}}
{{smaller block|In durance ''vile'' here must I wake and weep!
{{right|''Burns'', Epistle from Esopus to Maria.}}}}
{{smaller|='''Syn. 1.''' Contemptible, beggarly, pitiful, scurvy, shabby. —'''2.''' Groveling, ignoble, foul, knavish.}}
'''II.†''' ''n.'' A vile thing.
{{smaller block|Which soeuer of them I touche es a ''vyle''.
{{right|''Gosson'', Schoole of Abuse (ed. Arber), p. 25.}}}}

'''vile†''', ''v. t.'' [Early mod. E. also ''vyle''; < ''vile'', ''v.''] To make vile.
{{smaller block|I ''vyle'', I make vyle. Jauille, . . . Thou oughtest to be a shamed to ''vyle'' thy selfe with thyn yvell tonge.
{{right|''Palsgrave'', p. 765.}}}}

'''vilehead†''', ''n.'' [ME. ''vilehed''; < ''vile'' + ''-head''.] Vileness. {{smaller block|Huanne the man thength . . . and knauth his pourehede, the ''vilhede'', the brotelhede of his beringe [birth].
{{right|''Ayenbite of Inwyt'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 130.}}}}

'''vilein†, vileinie†.''' Obsolete spellings of ''villain'', ''villainy''.

'''vilely''' (vīl′li), ''adv.'' [Formerly also ''vildly''; < ME. ''villiche''; < ''vile'' + -''ly''<sup>2</sup>.] In a vile manner; basely; meanly; shamefully; abjectly; opprobriously; odiously; badly; wretchedly; worthlessly; sorrily.
{{smaller block|He speaks most ''vilely'' of you, like a foul-mouthed man as he is.
{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. IV., iii. 3. 122.}}}}

'''vileness''' (vīl′nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being vile. {{smaller|(''a'') Baseness; despicableness; meanness; contemptibleness; worthlessness.}}
{{smaller block|Considering the ''vileness'' of the clay, I have sometimes wondered that no tribune of that age durst ever venture to ask the potter, What dost thou make?
{{right|''Swift'', Nobles and Commons, v.}}}}
{{smaller|(''b'') Moral or intellectual deficiency; imperfection; depravity; degradation; impurity; wickedness; sinfulness; extreme badness.}}
{{smaller block|We, sensible of our corruption and ''vileness'', may be fearful and shy of coming near unto him.
{{right|''Barrow'', Sermons, I. vii.}}}}

'''vileyns†''', ''a.'' See ''villain''.

'''viliaco†''' (vil-i-ä′kō), ''n.'' [< It. ''vigliacco'', cowardly (= Sp. ''bellaco'' = Pg. ''velhaco'', low, bad), prob. < L. ''vilis'', vile: see ''vile''.] A villain; a scoundrel; a coward.
{{smaller block|Now out, base ''viliaco!''
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Every Man out of his Humour, v. 3.}}}}

'''vilicate†''' (vil′i-kāt), ''v. t.'' [Apparently an error for *''vilificate'' (see ''vilify'').] To defame; vilify.
{{smaller block|Baseness what it cannot attaine will ''vilicate'' and deprave.{{right|''R. Junius'', Cure of Misprision.}}}}

'''vilification''' (vil″i-fi-kā′shọn), ''n.'' [< LL. as if *''vilificatio''(''n''-), < ''vilificare'', pp. ''vilificatus'', make or esteem of little value: see ''vilify''.] The act of vilifying or defaming. ''Dr. H. More.''

'''vilifier''' (vil′i-fī-ėr), ''n.'' [< ''vilify'' + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] One who defames or traduces; a calumniator.

'''vilify''' (vil′i-fī), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''vilified'', ppr. ''vilifying''. [< LL. ''vilificare'', < L. ''vilis'', vile, + ''-ficare'', < ''facere'', make: see ''-fy''.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To make vile; debase; degrade.
{{smaller block|<poem>Their Maker’s image . . . then
Forsook them, when themselves they ''vilified''
To serve ungoverned appetite.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., xi. 516.}}
The wealth and pride of individuals at every moment makes the man of humble rank and fortune sensible of his inferiority, and degrades and ''vilifies'' his condition.
{{right|''Burke'', Rev. in France.}}}}
'''2.''' To attempt to degrade by slander; defame; traduce; calumniate.
{{smaller block|<poem>This Tomalin could not abide
To hear his sovereign ''vilified''.</poem>
{{right|''Drayton'', Nymphidia.}}}}
'''3†.''' To treat as worthless, vile, or of no account.
{{smaller block|You shall not finde our Saviour . . . so bent to contemn and ''vilifie'' a poor suitor.
{{right|''Hales'', Remains, Sermon on Luke xviii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller|='''Syn. 2.''' ''Asperse'', ''Defame'', ''Calumniate'', etc. (see ''asperse''), revile, abuse.}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To utter slander; be guilty of defamation. ''Rev. T. Adams'', Works, I. 153.

'''vilifying''' (vil′i-fī-ing), ''n.'' [Verbal n. of ''vilify'', ''v.''] The act of defaming or traducing; defamation; slander.
{{smaller block|In the midst of all the storms and reproaches and ''vilifyings'' that the world heaps upon me.
{{right|''Sir M. Hale'', Preparation against Afflictions.}}}}

'''vilipend''' (vil′i-pend), ''v.'' [< F. ''vilipender'' = It. ''vilipendere'' (cf. Sp. ''vilipendiar'', < ''vilipendio'', n.), < L. ''vilipendere'', hold of slight value, deprecate, deprive, < ''vilis'', of small price, + ''pendere'', weigh, weigh out: see ''vile'' and ''pendent''.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' To express a disparaging or mean opinion of; slander; vilify; treat slightingly or contemptuously.
{{smaller block|It is wicked to sell heavenly things at a great rate of worldly; but it is most wretched to ''vilipend'' them.
{{right|''Rev. T. Adams'', Works, I. 6.}}
Though I would by no means ''vilipend'' the study of the classicks.
{{right|''Lowell'', Biglow Papers, 2d ser., i.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To express disparaging opinions of a person; use vilification.
{{smaller block|It is profane and foolish to deify public opinion, or indeed anything; but it is not right, it is not safe to err on the other side, to ignore and ''vilipend''.
{{right|''Dr. J. Brown'', Spare Hours, 3d ser., p. 154.}}}}

'''vilipendency†''' (vil-i-pen′den-si), ''n.'' [< L. ''vilipenden(t-)s'', ppr. of ''vilipendere'': see ''vilipend'' and ''-cy''.] Disesteem; slight; disparagement. ''Bp. Hacket.''

'''vility†''' (vil′i-ti), ''n.'' [< ME. ''vilte'', ''vylte'', < OF. ''vilite'', ''viliteït'' = It. ''viltà'', < L. ''vilita(t-)s'', lowness of price, cheapness, worthlessness, < ''vilis'', cheap, worthless, vile: see ''vile''.] Vileness; baseness.
{{smaller block|In all his myghte purge he the ''vilte'' of syn in hyme and other.
{{right|''Hampole'', Prose Treatises (E. E. T. S.), p. 12.}}}}

'''vill''' (vil), ''n.'' [Also ''vil''; < ME. *''ville'' (only in legal use or in comp. in local names?), < OF. ''ville'', ''vile'', F. ''ville'', a village, town, city, = Sp. ''villa'', a town, a country house, = Pg. ''villa'', a village, town, = It. ''villa'', a country house, a farm, a village, also (after the F. and Sp.) a town, city, < L. ''villa'', a country house, a country-seat, a farm, villa; prob. a reduction of *''vicla'', dim. of ''vicus'', a village, etc., = Gr. οἶκος, a house: see ''wick''<sup>2</sup>, and cf. ''vicine'', ''vicinity'', etc. Hence ult. (< L. ''villa'') E. ''villa'' (a doublet of ''vill''), ''village'', ''villatic'', ''villain'', ''villainy'', etc. The word ''vill'' exists, chiefly in the form ''-ville'', as in French, in many names of towns, taken from or imitated from the French ''ville'', being practically an English formative applicable as freely as ''-burg'', ''-town'', or ''-ton'', in the United States, to the formation of local names from any surname, topographical name, or other term, as ''Brownsville'', ''Pottsville'', ''Jacksonville'', ''Yorkville'', ''Brookville'', ''Rockville'', ''Troutville'', ''Greenville'', ''Blackville'', ''Whiteville'', etc.] A hamlet or village; also, a manor; a parish; the outpart of a parish. (See ''village'', 2.) In old writings mention is made of ''entire vills'', ''demi-vills'', and ''hamlets''.
{{smaller block|Hence they were called villeins or villani—inhabitants of the ''vill'' or district. {{right|''Brougham'', Polit. Philos., I. 291.}}
For a long time the rectors of Whalley and of Blaghorn were for the most part married men, and the lords of ''vills''.
{{right|''De Statu Blaghornshire'', quoted in Baines’s Hist. Lancashire, II. 1.}}
<poem>
The tenantry of thorpe and ''vill'',
Or straggling burgh.
</poem>
{{right|''Wordsworth'', Excursion, viii.}}}}

'''Constable of vills.''' See ''constable'', 2.
